When something is commonplace, it means it is so ordinary, familiar, and frequently seen or heard that it no longer feels special, surprising, or worth noticing. It blends into the background of everyday life.

Think of it this way: if something is commonplace, the average person would respond to it with a shrug, not with wide eyes.

The word carries a quiet sense of lost novelty. Something becomes commonplace when it has been seen, heard, or experienced so many times — by so many people — that it no longer stands out. It is part of the furniture of normal life.

It's not just that the thing is ordinary. It's that it has become unremarkably ordinary. People don't stop to think about it. They don't comment on it. They simply expect it to be there.

• "Smartphones are commonplace now — almost everyone owns one."
    (Fifty years ago, this technology would have seemed like science fiction. Today, nobody is amazed by it.)
  • "Traffic jams are a commonplace occurrence in most big cities."
    (People expect them. They're a normal, boring fact of city life.)
  • "It has become commonplace for employees to work from home."
    (This was once unusual, but now it's so normal it barely deserves a mention.)
  • "Violence in action films has become so commonplace that audiences barely react to it anymore."
    (It happens so often that the shock value is completely gone.)
  • "He made the commonplace observation that hard work leads to success."
    (The remark was so obvious and so often repeated that it added nothing new.)
The subtle shade of meaning — slightly dismissive

This is an important nuance. When you call something commonplace, you are often implying — ever so gently — that it lacks originality, depth, or interest. It's not outright rude, but it does suggest the thing is unimpressive or unremarkable.

For example:

  • "Her speech was full of commonplace ideas" means her ideas were bland, recycled, and offered no fresh thinking.
  • "He had a commonplace mind" is actually a mild insult — it means the person thinks in ordinary, unimaginative ways.

This dismissive shade is not always present. When you say "electricity is commonplace in modern homes," you're simply stating a fact about how widespread it is. But when you say "the movie was filled with commonplace dialogue," you're criticizing it for being generic and unoriginal.

The key is context. You'll develop a feel for this with practice.

It helps to know what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean bad or low-quality. A commonplace thing may still be perfectly good. It's just not remarkable.
  • It does not mean rare. In fact, it's the opposite — commonplace things are everywhere.
  • It does not mean temporary. Something that is commonplace has typically settled into everyday life over time.

The clearest way to feel what commonplace means is to look at its opposites:

  • Extraordinary — far above the ordinary; exceptional
  • Remarkable — worthy of being noticed or commented upon
  • Rare — not seen or heard often
  • Novel — new and original
  • Unprecedented — never happened or existed before

If something is commonplace, it is the opposite of all these things.

Use "commonplace" when you want to describe something that:

  • has become so widespread or normal that it no longer attracts attention
  • lacks originality because it's been repeated too many times (ideas, phrases, plots)
  • was once special but has now faded into ordinary life

It fits well in formal and semi-formal writing, though you can use it in conversation too. It adds a certain precision and thoughtfulness to your language — more precise than just saying "normal" or "usual," because it carries the added sense of having lost any special quality through sheer repetition and familiarity.
